newsitem.title: UK: East Europe edges up in firm emerging debt market.
newsitem.headline: East Europe edges up in firm emerging debt market.

text.p: East Europe was the main focus of a relatively quiet and firm emerging debt market on Tuesday as the recent stability of U.S. Treasuries continues to prop up prices.
Russia and Bulgaria were both taken higher in morning trade, with some of the more exotic paper, notably Morocco and Nigeria, also catching up.
The resumption of the market rally, which has seen few interruptions since late last year, is encouraging scepticism among some traders who question whether spread tightening can go on much further.
But there are still plenty of others who see more space for prices to rise, though a potential U.S. rate hike in the near-term is a lingering concern.
One trader compared the current state of the market to its last bull run which ended in early 1994, turning into violent decline by the end of that year because of the Mexican peso crisis.
Russian Vneshekonombank dollar paper RUVNUSLNS=RR, the subject of at least one strong buy recommendation by a major bank, firmed to around a bid of 62-1/8 cents in the dollar.
MinFins were also firmer on local buying.
The market is, for the moment, fairly relaxed about the country's politics though President Boris Yeltsin's health is a relentless background worry, ahead of his heart operation later this month.

His press secretary earlier announced that while he was away from the Kremlin, Yeltsin had put Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin -- a favourite of foreign investors -- in charge of ministries involved with defence, secutiry and foreign affairs.
Bulgaria, a fairly thin market, was also firmer and traders said its recent plunge had lured back some investors, attracted by its high yield.
One European bank trader noted some buying of uncollaterised Bulgarian IABs BGFLTH11=RR and selling of collaterised discount Bradys BGFLTH24A=RR.
Elsewhere, Algeria was firmer, up around its highest so far this year, while Nigerian paper has also risen sharply this week, possibly on the back of the recent rise in oil prices.
